query: Which quasi-experimental designs (propensity-score matching, difference-in-differences) most robustly attribute curriculum effects when RCTs are infeasible?

response.query: Which quasi-experimental designs (propensity-score matching, difference-in-differences) most robustly attribute curriculum effects when RCTs are infeasible?
response.answer: Propensity-score matching and difference-in-differences are the most robust quasi-experimental designs for attributing curriculum effects when RCTs are infeasible.

results.title: Introduction to Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Design
results.content: # Introduction to Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Design Part of the book series: Springer Texts in Education ((SPTE)) ## Abstract This chapter introduces readers to main concepts in experimental and quasi-experimental design. First, randomized control trials are introduced as the primary example of experimental design. Next, nonexperimental contexts, and particularly the use of propensity score matching to approximate the conditions of randomized control trials, are described. Finally, this chapter introduces two quasi-experimental design that are particularly useful in international education research: regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences. In such situations, quasi-experimental techniques like difference-in-difference, regression discontinuity, and synthetic controls can be used to estimate the causal impact of the treatment. It is comprised of three techniques: defining an adopter, propensity score matching and difference-in-difference (DiD). Propensity score matching is a technique that aims to minimize selection bias by creating comparison groups with similar observed characteristics. Propensity score matching is based on the probability of treatment assignment, given observed baseline covariates, such as demographics, prior engagement with the platform, and tenure. We would match two members from the treatment and control groups, respectively, based on their propensity scores, which should be within a specified threshold. For categorical variables, we look at plots comparing the proportional differences between test and control before and after matching. For continuous variables, we look at Empirical Cumulative Distribution Functions (ECDF) for our test and control groups before and after matching. control or adopter / non-adopter propensity distributions before matching. As we can see in the chart, the test and control groups (adopters and non-adopters) are already separable before matching, which means matching is required to account for confounding variables and get an accurate estimate of the true treatment effect. Once we have matched the treatment and control groups on observed characteristics, we can then use difference-in-difference to estimate causal impact. By using matching before applying DiD, we take care of the assumption that treatment group and control group must follow the same trend in the pre-period. In the price discount example, we would simply compare changes in spend, basket size and retention over time in the treatment group to changes in control group. Aggregating the matched pairs from the treatment and control groups, we calculate the difference-in-difference estimate, i.e., the Average Treatment Effect (ATE):. Thus, the combination of defining adopters, propensity score matching, and difference-in-difference can make more robust inferences than the individual techniques when randomization is not feasible.
